Early transition metal carbides (for example Mo2C, WC, TiC, VC, NbC and TaC) are hard, refractory compounds in which carbon occupies interstitial sites of a metal lattice. They have been studied as catalysts since reports of "platinum-like" activity, and a central question is how carbon modifies the electronic structure and reactivity of the parent metal surface, which depends strongly on surface termination.

## DFT trends on Mo2C and rocksalt carbide surfaces (2005)

Kitchin, Nørskov, Barteau and Chen used PW91 DFT to study β-Mo2C(0001) and the (111) surfaces of TiC, VC, NbC and TaC. Bulk lattice constants and bulk moduli agreed well with experiment, and first-layer contraction on metal-terminated surfaces was reproduced. Carbon did not change the d-electron count of surface Mo (6.45 to 6.69 versus 6.47 for Mo(110)), so it does not make Mo Pt-like by electron donation. Metal-terminated carbide surfaces bound atomic H more strongly than the parent metals (except VC), attributed to tensile strain from the expanded metal-metal distances, while carbon-terminated surfaces bound H more weakly at some sites and formed very stable C-H species (3.92 eV on TaC(111)). The authors suggest surface carbon passivates the metal and that defect chemistry and carbon participation in reactions matter ([Kitchin et al. 2005](/papers/kitchin2005/)). Summary: [kitchin2005](/papers/kitchin2005/).

## Metal-modified Mo2N for selective isopropanol bond scission (2024)

Porter and coworkers extended the metal-modified carbide approach to the nitride analogue Mo2N, using isopropanol as a probe of C−O, C−H and C−C scission. Unmodified Mo2N favored dehydration to propylene (about 59% selectivity in TPD, 60% on powders at 413 K), whereas Fe and Pt overlayers suppressed dehydration; Pt/Mo2N powders were 93.4% selective to acetone. DFT on N-terminated γ-Mo2N(111) traced the dehydration preference to the strong oxygen affinity of surface Mo (O binding energy −3.79 eV), which stabilizes an O-anchored isopropoxy that then loses its oxygen, while a Pt monolayer on Mo2N binds O at only −1.31 eV and behaves like Pt(111) ([Porter et al. 2024](/papers/porter2024/)). Summary: [porter2024](/papers/porter2024/).
